{\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace works as follows: It
is parameterized by a \emph{learning rate} $\eta$, and an
\emph{exploration probability} $\gamma$. It maintains a set of weights
$w_{s}$, one for each arm (sensor) $s$, initialized to
1. 
At every round $t$,
it will select each arm $s$ with probability
$$p_{s}=(1-\gamma)\frac{w_{s}}{\sum_{s'}
  w_{s'}}+\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}},$$ i.e., with probability $\gamma$
it explores, picking an arm uniformly at random, and with probability
$(1-\gamma)$ it exploits, picking an arm $s$ with probability
proportional to its weight $w_{s}$.  Once an arm $s$ has been
selected, a feedback $r=\ensuremath{f}_{t}(\{s\})$ is obtained, and the weight $w_{s}$ is
updated to
$$w_{s}\leftarrow w_{s}\exp(\eta r/p_{s}).$$ 
Auer et al.~\cite{auer02} showed that
with appropriately chosen learning rate $\eta$ and exploration
probability $\gamma$ it holds that the cumulative regret $R_{T}$ of
{\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T \ensuremath{n} \ln \ensuremath{n} })$, i.e., the
average regret $R_{T}/T$ converges to zero.

Lazy renormalization
selects each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, because of the way the random bits
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for
sensor activation and selection.
Note that it would be sufficient to run the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace on the correct (possibly
oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, 
since then~Prop.~\ref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\ensuremath{v}$
is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
The difficulty is that $\ensuremath{v}$ does not have access to the correct
normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it,
$Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability
distribution over two random variables $(X_{\ensuremath{v}},
Y_{\ensuremath{v}})$, where 
\[
X_{\ensuremath{v}}  = X_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}  \right.
\]
\[
Y_{\ensuremath{v}} = Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda}
    \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R }
\]
and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is
sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.
Now, note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}$ is distributed as $\Poisson{\lambda}$.
Also note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$,
because $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $R \ge e^{-\lambda}$ and 
\[
 e^{-\lambda}  \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))
\]
since $1 + x \le e^x$ for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and $\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),
Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact
that $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \le Z(t)$.
It follows that we can use the event $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ as a
conservative indicator that $\ensuremath{v}$ should activate.
In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and its weight $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to the server.  
The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can
use $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ and $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to compute
$Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(r_{\ensuremath{v}})$, 
the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\ensuremath{v}$ would have
drawn had it known $Z(t)$.  The resulting distribution on selected
sensors is thus exactly the same as in the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace without lazy
renormalization.
Invoking~Prop.~\ref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof.
